questions.q: Which of the following correctly lists the four G4 nations jointly advocating for permanent UN Security Council membership?
questions.a: Correct answer: India, Brazil, Germany, Japan. A wrong answer (e.g., including South Africa or Nigeria) reveals the student confuses G4 with the African Union's Ezulwini Consensus position (two permanent seats for Africa) or the broader "Uniting for Consensus" group (Italy, Pakistan, Mexico, etc.) which opposes new permanent seats. This distinction is critical because G4 coordinates as a bloc, while African Group and UfC have different reform proposals.

questions.q: Explain why India argues that 'historical responsibility' and 'capacity to contribute' — not just economic size — justify its claim to a permanent UNSC seat. Use two specific examples from India's UN track record.
questions.a: Correct answer: India's claim rests on (1) normative leadership: co-sponsoring 1960 Declaration on Granting Independence to Colonial Countries (Resolution 1514), chairing Decolonization Committee, and (2) material contribution: largest cumulative troop contributor to UN peacekeeping (over 250,000 personnel since 1948), with 179 fatalities — highest of any nation. A wrong answer citing only GDP or population reveals the student misses the dual moral-material logic India deploys: the UN Charter (Article 23) criteria for UNSC membership explicitly include 'contribution to maintenance of international peace and security' — which India meets through peacekeeping, not just economic weight.

questions.q: India has served 8 terms as a non-permanent UNSC member (latest 2021-22). In a hypothetical scenario where India is a permanent member with veto, analyze how India's voting behavior on the 2022 Ukraine resolution (S/RES/2623) would likely differ from its actual abstention — and why.
questions.a: Correct analysis: As non-permanent member, India abstained on the procedural vote to refer Ukraine to General Assembly (S/RES/2623) — balancing strategic autonomy (not condemning Russia) with territorial integrity principles. As permanent member with veto, India would likely still abstain or vote against any resolution authorizing force under Chapter VII, because: (a) veto is a shield against unwanted interventionism, not a tool for active blocking; (b) India's historical position opposes coercive regime change (see 2011 Libya abstention on Resolution 1973); (c) permanent status would strengthen India's 'strategic autonomy' narrative — veto becomes a deterrent against Western pressure. A wrong answer assuming India would 'use veto to protect Russia' reveals misunderstanding: India uses veto/abstention to preserve decision-making sovereignty, not as a transactional tool for allies.

questions.q: Compare the 'G4 model' of UNSC expansion (new permanent members with veto) vs. the 'Uniting for Consensus / Coffee Club model' (new non-permanent seats only). Identify the core structural disagreement and explain why the Coffee Club opposes G4 — using the specific cases of Italy vs. Germany and Pakistan vs. India.
questions.a: Correct analysis: Core disagreement is whether new permanent members get veto power. G4 demands veto (or phased veto after review); UfC (Italy, Pakistan, Mexico, South Korea, etc.) opposes any new permanent seats, proposing only longer-term non-permanent seats. Italy opposes Germany's bid (regional rival, WWII legacy); Pakistan opposes India's bid (Kashmir dispute, parity obsession). UfC argues new permanent seats entrench inequality; G4 argues current P5 monopoly is the real inequality. A wrong answer saying 'UfC opposes reform' is false — UfC supports reform but of a different kind. This distinction matters because General Assembly resolution requires 2/3 majority — UfC's 40+ members can block G4.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of India's strategy of linking UNSC reform to broader 'Global South' leadership (Voice of Global South Summit 2023, G20 presidency 2023) versus the traditional G4-only diplomatic track. Which approach has yielded more tangible outcomes since 2020?
questions.a: Correct evaluation: G20/Global South track has yielded more tangible outcomes: (1) African Union admitted as permanent G20 member (2023) — template for UNSC; (2) India's G20 presidency produced New Delhi Declaration with consensus on UN reform language ('more representative, inclusive, effective'); (3) Voice of Global South Summit created 125-nation coalition amplifying reform demand. G4 track remains stalled — no Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) text adopted since 2008. However, G4 track maintains institutional pressure within UNGA. A wrong answer claiming 'G4 got closer to seat' ignores reality: no IGN text, P5 (especially China) vetoes any expansion including India. The Global South strategy builds normative consensus outside UNSC — where P5 veto doesn't apply.

questions.q: Draft a 3-point reform proposal for the IMF quota system that reflects India's long-standing position (since 2010 Quota Reforms) — specifying: (a) the metric shift needed, (b) the protection for poorest members, and (c) the governance change for Executive Board composition.
questions.a: Expected answer: (a) Shift from GDP-weighted quotas to PPP-GDP + openness + variability + reserves formula (2010 Reform package) — increasing emerging economies' share by 6%+; (b) Protect IDA-eligible (poorest) countries' voting share via 'ad hoc quota increase' — India supported this in 2010; (c) Move to fully elected Executive Board (no appointed Directors for top quota holders) — India advocates this to end US/European monopoly on Managing Director/Deputy MD posts. A poor answer proposing 'just give India more votes' misses the systemic principle: India argues for rules-based formula protecting vulnerable, not ad hoc bargains. This mirrors India's UNSC stance: reform by criteria, not patronage.
